query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Scandium to high-entropy alloys based on refractory metals enhances superconductivity by promoting the formation of a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase, which is rich in Scandium and Zirconium, and poor in Tantalum and Niobium.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys based on refractory metals, such as Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr, in their as-cast state.
generation.intervention: Addition of Scandium to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloys are synthesized using arc melting in an Ar atmosphere and are characterized using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase, which is rich in Scandium and Zirconium, and poor in Tantalum and Niobium.
generation.mechanism: The Scandium addition promotes the formation of the hcp phase, which has a higher superconducting transition temperature than the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys will exhibit enhanced superconductivity compared to the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr parent alloys.
generation.baseline: The superconducting properties of the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr parent alloys, as reported in literature.
generation.boundary: The alloys are limited to those with a refractory metal base and a high-entropy composition, and the Scandium addition is limited to a few percent.
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which Scandium enhances superconductivity in these alloys is not fully understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the superconducting transition temperature of the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys and compare it to that of the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr parent alloys.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys do not exhibit enhanced superconductivity compared to the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr parent alloys, the hypothesis is falsified.

The applications of refractory metals include tools to work metallic materials, wire filaments, casting molds and chemical reaction vessels in corrosive environments. Strong resistance against mechanical forces at high temperatures makes them potentially suitable for the application in jet engines and as tools used during forging. Shortcomings are poor low-temperature workability and extreme oxidability at high temperatures. Interaction with the environment can also significantly reduce the high-temperature creep strength, so that the application often requires protective atmosphere or coating. To overcome these shortfalls, refractory elements are frequently alloyed with other refractory elements, occasionally with an addition of a non-refractory element (such as Al). When five or more elements are alloyed in near-equimolar concentrations, crystalline random solid solutions or partially ordered ones may sometimes form, termed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [,]. A well-studied refractory HEA system is Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr, which demonstrates decent RT ductility and solid solution strengthening at high temperatures [,,

Sc has also been incorporated as one of the principal elements into equimolar AlCrCuScTi HEA [], where it was observed that the formation and degradation of the Al3Sc, Al2Cu3Sc and Al4Cu4Sc intermetallic precipitates upon heating plays a crucial role in the record high value of the hardness/density ratio of this alloy, in comparison with ordinary heavy refractory HEAs. ## 2.1. X-ray Diffraction
XRD patterns of the investigated alloys are presented in Figure 1. Towards the edges, a fine dispersion of much smaller precipitates of the two phases (bright and dark), mostly of 10–100 nm dimensions, is evident on the sub-micron scale. The dark interdendritic regions, enriched in lighter elements, are even more inhomogeneous. There are no large (µm-size) regions of either of the two phases, but the microstructure is more mottled, containing finely intermixed bright and dark precipitates of the two phases (of spherical-like or elongated shape), again of 10–100 nm dimensions. The dark precipitates occupy considerably larger fraction of the interdendritic regions than the bright ones. The interdendritic regions can be viewed as eutectic mixtures.

By also analyzing the EDS elemental maps of other alloys, we found that the following composition pattern is commonly appearing in all alloys: the bright dendrites are Ta- and Nb-rich, but poor in Sc and Zr, whereas the opposite holds true for the dark interdendritic regions, which are Sc- and Zr-rich, but Ta- and Nb-poor. The dark phase absorbs practically all Sc. Hf and Ti are quite uniformly distributed over the two phases. The fact that Sc “likes” Zr, but strongly repels Ta and Nb, whereas Hf and Ti mix well with all elements, is in agreement with the qualitative predictions based on the binary mixing enthalpies from Table 2. The considerable amount of Ta detected in the interdendritic regions of some alloys (up to 15 at.%) does not prove its inclusion into the dark phase, but rather reflects fine dispersion of the dark and bright sub-micron precipitates that are simultaneously hit by the electron beam in the EDS experiment.
